system:
You are an experienced litigator who has supervised many document reviews. You
are asked to estimate, item by item, how hard it is for a human reviewer to
check one call, and to say why.

### The reviewer's task

The reviewer is law-trained but not a specialist in the case's industry, and
**has already read and understood this case**: the opinion, the contracts, and
every court defect — each provision the court construed, and for each one every
distinct defect the court construed in it, with the passage of the opinion it
comes from.

They are now given a list of **items**. Each item is one description of a
defect, written by someone else about one provision the court construed, and
the call a first reader made on it. The call is one of two kinds:

- **A match.** The first reader said the description names one particular court
  defect on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether it does — whether
  the description and that court defect are about the same words and the same
  problem with them — and not some other court defect, or none.
- **No match.** The first reader said the description names none of the court
  defects on that provision. The reviewer must decide whether that is right —
  whether the description fails to name each one of them.

You are judging **how hard it is to reach that decision** for each item. Not
whether the first reader was right: do not decide that, and do not let a view
on it set the difficulty. Not how hard the case is: the reviewer already knows
the case, so count only the work this item adds.

### What does not count

- **How hard the case is.** Two items in one case can differ widely. Rate each
  item by what checking it takes on top of an understanding of the case.
- **The number of items.** Each item is rated on its own, and an item does not
  get easier or harder because there are many others.
- **Length by itself.** A long description is hard only where its length makes
  it unclear what it names.
- **How close the description is to the court defect.** A full match, a clear
  partial match and a clear mismatch are all easy to check. Difficulty is how
  hard it is to **see** how close they are, not how close they turn out to be.
- **Wording.** A description that calls the court's problem by another name —
  "indefinite" where the court said "ambiguous", "open-ended" where it said
  "unclear" — about the same words is no harder to check than one that uses
  the court's own word.
- **Distinctions the court did not draw.** Two framings of what is wrong with
  the same words — its meaning is uncertain, its reach is too broad — can be
  told apart in theory. A reviewer does not stop over that unless **the court's
  construction turned on it**: unless the court accepted one framing and
  rejected the other, or decided the case on a point one framing reaches and
  the other misses. Where the court did not, the reviewer sees the same words
  and the same kind of complaint, and confirms the call at a glance.

### How a reviewer actually checks an item

To check an item the reviewer has to settle, in turn:

1. **What the description is about** — which words, which other provision or
   document, and what it says is wrong with them;
2. **whether each thing it asserts is true** — what the contract says, what a
   term or a document is, what happened between the parties;
3. **whether that is what the court construed** — the same words, and the
   point the court's construction actually turned on;
4. **whether the call follows** — given all that, does the description name the
   matched court defect, or none of them.

An item is easy when every step is quick and the answer to each is plain. It is
hard when a step cannot be finished from the clause and the passage, or when,
with every step done, it is still not plain what the answer is.

### What makes an item easy to check

The comparison is clear-cut, whichever way it comes out:

- **One phrase, one step.** The description points at a phrase of the clause
  and says what is wrong with it in one step — this phrase is vague, this term
  is undefined — and the court construed that phrase for that reason. The
  reviewer reads the description once and confirms it against the passage.
- **Plainly different.** The description is about other words, or a different
  problem, so the mismatch is seen just as quickly.
- **Anything extra is plainly separate.** Where the description also raises a
  point about another clause, term or objection, that point is set aside at a
  glance; it does not need to be checked to decide the call.
- **Nothing to verify.** What the description asserts can be seen in the
  clause and the passage themselves.
- **The provision has one court defect**, or its court defects are clearly
  separate, so there is only one comparison to make.

An item like that takes a minute or two, and the reviewer ends confident.

### What makes an item hard to check

What makes an item hard is that **a step cannot be settled from the clause and
the passage, or the answer stays unclear once it is**. Each of these adds time,
and they compound:

- **The two sides may name the same thing differently.** The description
  refers to a document, a party, a transaction or a category of things by one
  name, and the court by another, and whether they are the same thing is a
  question of fact — about the deal, the record or the industry — that the
  reviewer has to look up before the comparison can even start.
- **The description makes claims that have to be verified.** It asserts facts
  about the contract, the parties, a court or a body, a document or the
  background, and the reviewer has to check them against the contract, the
  opinion or outside knowledge. Some may turn out to be wrong.
- **It bundles several claims about the same defect, some of them doubtful.**
  The description makes several points about the same words or the same
  dispute; some look right and some look wrong. The reviewer has to grade each
  and then decide whether the call stands on the right ones.
- **It has the right words but not the court's point.** The description is
  about the words the court construed, but misses, or misstates, a point the
  court's construction actually turned on — one the opinion relies on, not one
  a reader could merely imagine. The reviewer has to decide whether that still
  names the court defect, and even with every fact checked, careful reviewers
  can disagree.
- **Its reasoning runs over several steps.** The description reaches its defect
  through a chain — this term, read with that provision, given this fact — and
  the reviewer has to follow and test each link.
- **The defect is relational and the description has only part of it.** The
  court's defect lies in how this provision is read with another provision or
  with a separate document, and the description addresses only this one, or
  only one side of the relationship, so the reviewer has to decide how much of
  the relationship it must reach before it counts.
- **The description is vague or general.** It could be read as naming the court
  defect or as naming something near it, and the reviewer has to decide how
  much it must say before it counts.
- **Several court defects on the provision are close to one another**, so the
  description could name one, another, or more than one of them, and the
  reviewer has to tell them apart before they can check the call.

An item like that can take half an hour or more, and the reviewer may still be
unsure at the end.

### The scale

- **`difficulty`** — `easy`, `intermediate` or `hard`.
- **`score`** — an integer from 1 to 10, and use the whole range. 1–3 is easy:
  1–2 when the decision is plain at a glance, 3 when one more look is needed.
  4–6 is intermediate: a claim to verify or a framing to work through, but the
  answer is plain once that is done. 7–10 is hard: 9–10 when, with every claim
  checked, two careful reviewers could still decide it differently.
  `difficulty` and `score` must agree.
- **`estimated_minutes`** — your estimate of how long the reviewer needs to
  reach a decision on this item, given that they already understand the case.
  Count only the work this item adds.
instructions:
Work in this order.

1. **Read the court defects** in the task and the provisions they sit in, until
   you could say what each one is about in a sentence.
2. **Go through the items one at a time.** For each one, read the description,
   then the court defects on its provision, then the call, and walk the four
   steps a reviewer takes: what the description is about, whether what it
   asserts is true, whether that is what the court construed, whether the call
   follows. Note which step takes work, what that work needs — the clause, the
   rest of the contract, the opinion, outside facts — and whether its answer is
   plain once the work is done.
3. **Rate the item by how clear that comparison is** — not by how close the
   description turns out to be, not by how hard the case is, and not by whether
   you think the call is right.

Return exactly one entry per item, under its id, in the order given.

In each `reason`, give one or two sentences specific to this item: name the
step that takes the work, and the words, claim or court defect it turns on.
task:
### The court defects in 68 F.Supp.3d 317

### Contract 68FSupp3d317_2008_agreement

The court construed no provision of this contract.

### Contract 68FSupp3d317_2009_agreement

#### c006 — 2. TERM OF AGREEMENT

```
2. TERM OF AGREEMENT Subject to Section 12 of this Agreement, this Agreement shall become effective as of the date hereof and shall continue until December 31, 2010, and shall continue in effect until either party terminates this agreement by providing the other party with written notice of termination at least ninety (90) days prior to such termination. DISTRIBUTOR shall have the right to enter into consecutive successor DSDD Distributor Agreements unless this (or any applicable successor) Agreement has been terminated or unless DISTRIBUTOR has committed a material breach of this (or any applicable successor) Agreement which remains outstanding as of the date that DISTRIBUTOR notifies COMPANY of its desire to enter into a successor Agreement (as specified below) and which material breach COMPANY has not waived. The term of the first successor DSDD Distributor Agreement shall commence on the date that this Agreement expires, and the term of each successor DSDD Distributor Agreement shall begin on the date that the applicable predecessor DSDD Distributor Agreement expires. If DISTRIBUTOR wishes to exercise its w right to enter into a successor DSDD Distributor Agreements, it will do so by executing COMPANY’S then-current form of DSDD Distributor Agreement, the terms of which may differ from the terms of this Agreement.
```

- **d01** (risk type 1.1, scope `clause`): The phrase “Subject to Section 12” was lexically unclear in scope because Premier read it to condition all Section 2 termination rights, while Kellogg read it to modify only the clause continuing the agreement through December 31, 2010.
  Opinion lines 89-93:
```
Here, Section 2 of the 2009 Agreement states, “Subject to Section 12 of this Agreement, this Agreement shall become effective as of the date hereof and shall continue until December 31, 2010, and shall continue in effect until either party terminates this agreement by providing the other party with written notice of termination at least ninety (90) days prior to such termination.” (Ceruto Decl., Ex. A, at 1.) (emphasis added).
Courts have interpreted the “subject to” to impose a “condition precedent.” See Cranpark, Inc. v. Rogers Grp., Inc., 721 F.Supp.2d 613, 627 (N.D.Ohio 2010) rev’d on other grounds, 498 Fed.Appx. 563 (6th Cir.2012) (“The language ‘SUBJECT TO RGI SR. MGT. APPROVAL’ clearly imposes a condition precedent.”); 13 Williston on Contracts § 38:16 (4th ed.) (“Likewise, the words ‘subject to’ in a contract usually indicate a condition to one party’s duty of performance and not a promise by the other.”). Under New York law, a “condition precedent is an act or event, other than a lapse of time, which, unless the condition is excused, must occur before a duty to perform a promise in the agreement arises.” Edelman Arts, Inc. v. Art Int’l (UK) Ltd., 841 F.Supp.2d 810, 823 (S.D.N.Y.2012) (quoting Oppenheimer & Co. v. Oppenheim, Appel, Dixon & Co., 86 N.Y.2d 685, 636 N.Y.S.2d 734, 660 N.E.2d 415, 418 (1995)).
Here, the parties agree that “Subject to Section 12” imposes a condition precedent. However, they disagree as to how broadly the parties intended for it to apply to the termination rights set forth in Section 2. The Plaintiff contends that the parties intended the language, “Subject to Section 12,” to make all of the termination rights set forth in Section 2 subject to the conditions set forth in Section 12. (The Pl.’s Mem. of Law at 10.) The Defendant argues that the parties only intended, “Subject to Section 12,” to apply to the first clause of the first sentence in Section 2, “this Agreement shall become effective as of the date hereof shall continue until December 31, 2010,” and not the second clause, “and shall continue in effect until either party terminates this agreement by providing the other party with written notice of termination at least ninety (90) days prior to. such termination.” (The Def.’s Mem. of Law at 10.)
The Court notes that at first blush, both parties’ interpretations appear plausible. However, several cannons of construction militate toward adopting the Defendant’s interpretation. In particular, when faced with two interpretations of a provision, courts generally prefer the narrower interpretation absent a clear manifestation of intent. Bank of New York v. Amoco Oil Co., 35 F.3d 643, 662 (2d Cir.1994) (“Where one interpretation is broader than another, courts should not apply the broader interpretation absent a clear manifestation of intent.”).
Here, the Plaintiffs interpretation of “Subject to Section 12” is broader than the Defendant’s interpretation because the Plaintiff contends that the parties intended this language to make all of the termination rights discussed in Section 2 “subservient” to the specific conditions for termination described in Section 12. (The Pl.’s Mem. of Law at 10.) The Defendant contends that the parties only intended “Subject to Section 12” to apply to the first clause of the sentence describing the parties termination rights through December 31, 2010. Therefore, the Court is inclined to adopt the Defendant’s more narrow interpretation of Section 2.
```

- **d02** (risk type 2.2, scope `contract`): Section 2 presented a whole-contract coherence problem because applying “Subject to Section 12” to its post-2010 termination right would eliminate the general right to terminate on 90 days’ notice and render that language meaningless or superfluous.
  Opinion lines 94-96:
```
More importantly, the Plaintiffs interpretation of “Subject to Section 12” would render the second clause of the first sentence of Section 2 meaningless. In particular, the second clause of this sentence provides that the Agreement “shall continue in effect until either party terminates this agreement by providing the other party with written notice of termination at least ninety (90) days prior to such termination.” In other words, this clause gives either party the right to terminate the 2009 Agreement for any reason upon 90 days’ written notice. If this clause were made “[s]ubject to Section 12,” it would eliminate that general termination right because Section 12 only permits a party to terminate, the 2009 Agreement under two limited circumstances — “for good cause” or “a change in COMPANY’S business that results in COMPANY no longer using Independent DSDD distributors in this territory.” Therefore, making the second clause of the first sentence of Section 2 “[s]ubject to Section 12” would render it superfluous.
Indeed, at oral argument, Kaufmann appeared to concede that his interpretation would render much of the language in Section 2 superfluous: “[T]he changes [the Defendant] made in that first sentence, the one that says, it will continue in effect until either party terminates this agreement, by providing 90 days’ notice, but that’s all subject to section 12. The rest of the language [in Section 2], Judge, is just carryover language now which is — was rendered superfluous by the change that [the Defendant] made.” (Dec. 13, 2014 Oral Argument Tr. 30:5-17.) (emphasis added).
On the other hand, the Defendant’s interpretation gives effect to all of the language in Section 2 of the 2009 Agreement by making termination subject to the conditions set forth in “Section 12” until December 31, 2010, while preserving the parties’ right to terminate the agreement upon 90 days’ written notice for any reason after December 31, 2010. See Ferguson v. Hannover Ruckversicherungs-Akteiengesellschaft, No. 04 CIV. 9254(PKL), 2007 WL 2493692, at *14 (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 21, 2007) (“Courts will not interpret a contract or a provision of a contract so as to leave the contract or provision ‘without force and effect.’ ”) (citation omitted).
```

#### c053 — 12(i). Termination on notice

```
12, (i) TERMINATION This Agreement may be terminated by either party at any time upon ninety (90) days written notice to the other for good cause (defined as either party’s breach of this Agreement which is not cured within those times specified below) or a change in COMPANY ’s business that results in COMPANY no longer using Independent DSDD distributors in this territory, with the date of yf (il) (ili) termination to be set forth in the notice or by mutual agreement.
```

- **d03** (risk type 2.2, scope `contract`): Section 12’s limited termination rights for good cause or a change in Kellogg’s business raised a whole-contract coherence question with Section 2, which the court resolved by treating Section 12’s expedited for-cause remedy and Section 2’s post-2010 no-cause 90-day remedy as distinct and harmonious.
  Opinion lines 97-98:
```
In response, the Plaintiff contends that the Defendant’s interpretation of Section 2 would render Section 12 of the Agreement superfluous. (The Pl.’s Reply Mem. of Law at 10.) The Court disagrees.
Construing -Section 2 to, afford either party the right to terminate the 2009 Agreement without cause after December 31, 2010 does not affect or otherwise inhibit a party’s right to terminate the 2009 Agreement based on the conditions set forth in Section 12 at any point after the Agreement becomes effective. See Morse/Diesel, Inc. v. Trinity Indus., Inc., 67 F.3d 435, 439 (2d Cir.1995) (“[T]he entire contract must be considered, and all parts of it reconciled, if possible, in order to avoid an inconsistency.”) (quoting Cruden v. Bank of New York, 957 F.2d 961, 976 (2d Cir.1992)). For example, Section 12(iii) gives the Defendant the right to terminate the Agreement if the Plaintiff fails to cure a material breach after five days written notice. (Ceruto Deck, Ex. A, at 11.) If the Court were to adopt the Defendant’s interpretation of Section 2, the Defendant would have (i) the right to terminate the 2009 Agreement within five days under Section 12 if the Plaintiff fails to cure a material breach; and (ii) have the right terminate the 2009 Agreement pursuant to Section 2 of the Agreement on 90 days’ notice without cause after December 31, 2010. There is nothing inconsistent about affording the Defendant the right to terminate the 2009 Agreement under these distinct and separate circumstances. Indeed, interpreting the 2009 Agreement in this way is consistent with the requirement that the Court make a “reasonable effort ... to harmonize all of its terms.” See India.Com, Inc. v. Dalal, 412 F.3d 315, 323 (2d Cir.2005); see also Cameron Int’l Trading Co. v. Hawk Importers, Inc., No. 03-CV-02496 (JS), 2010 WL 4568980, at *4 (E.D.N.Y. Nov. 2, 2010) aff'd, 501 Fed.Appx. 36 (2d Cir.2012) (“Effect and meaning must be given to every term of the contract, and reasonable effort must be made to harmonize all of its terms.”).
```


### The items to rate

#### a01

On `68FSupp3d317_2009_agreement` c006 — 2. TERM OF AGREEMENT. Court defects on this provision: d01, d02.

The description:
```
The term clause says the Agreement "shall continue until December 31, 2010, and shall continue in effect until either party terminates," so it is unclear whether the Agreement expires on that date or renews indefinitely subject only to ninety days' notice. The phrase "at least ninety (90) days prior to such termination" also leaves open who fixes the termination date.
```

The first reader matched it to **none** of d01, d02.

#### a02

On `68FSupp3d317_2009_agreement` c006 — 2. TERM OF AGREEMENT. Court defects on this provision: d01, d02.

The description:
```
Section 2 permits either party to end the Agreement on ninety days' written notice without stating any cause, while Section 12(i) permits termination on ninety days' notice only "for good cause" or on a change in COMPANY's business. A court would have to decide whether termination without cause is permitted, notwithstanding the "Subject to Section 12" opening words.
```

The first reader matched it to **d02**.

#### a03

On `68FSupp3d317_2009_agreement` c053 — 12(i). Termination on notice. Court defects on this provision: d03.

The description:
```
Section 12(i) permits termination on ninety days' notice only "for good cause" or on a change in COMPANY's business, which cannot be squared with Section 2's provision that the Agreement continues "until either party terminates ... by providing ... written notice of termination at least ninety (90) days prior." Whether termination without cause was available is the central construction question.
```

The first reader matched it to **d03**.

One entry per item above, each under its id.
